2.text: During my travels I had much trouble with women on account of the

3.text: fire. Many of them had no teakettles of their own, and yet refused to boil

4.text: water in mine because it had stood by an alien hearth. Sometimes their

5.text: scruples would give way at the prospect of drinking hot tea. In other cases

6.text: we had to make a separate fire, and drink our tea outside of the tent.

7.text: Brothers, cousins, and relatives of male descent, while living in the same

8.text: camp, or at least in the same neighborhood, may freely interchange fire. If

9.text: one of them has moved to a distant country, his fire gradually becomes

10.text: estranged from the primary hearth, because it consumes strange fuel, and

11.text: inhales alien and unseemly odors. In this way, even brothers who have been

12.text: separated for a long term of years may lose the right to interchange their fires.

13.text: When there are two or more fires of different family descent in the same

14.text: camp, a community fire may result, if the children playing together should

15.text: happen to mix one fire with another. The respective families will then bring

16.text: a common sacrifice, and for the future will keep up a common fire. The

17.text: community of related people who use fire from a common source are called

18.text: “those having the same fire” (ᴇnnaˊn-yɪˊnlɪt). This term is equivalent to another
18.resolved: ᴇ = U+1D07 LATIN LETTER SMALL CAPITAL E; ˊ = U+02CA MODIFIER LETTER ACUTE ACCENT (stress, x2); ɪ = U+026A LATIN LETTER SMALL CAPITAL I (dotless, x2)
18.note: Parenthetical gloss word-initial capital is a small-cap ᴇ (§2.3 series ᴀ ᴇ ɪ ʟ), clearly shorter than ascender-height letters on the same line (contrast: 'This' a few words later). Two raised marks read as stress U+02CA per §5.8/§4 default.

19.text: one which designates kinship in the male line, — “old buck-fellow community”

20.resolved: ɪ = U+026A LATIN LETTER SMALL CAPITAL I (dotless, x2); ñ = n + U+0303 COMBINING TILDE; ˊ = U+02CA MODIFIER LETTER ACUTE ACCENT (stress, x2)
20.note: Checked the 'g' in 'mgɪ' at 4x for a dot below (§5.1 prior runs toward g̣): no dot visible, keyed bare g.

21.text: Most of the camps have a common fire because their inhabitants belong

22.text: to related families. Difficulties regarding the fire arise in the camps of rich

23.text: reindeer-breeders, who hire poor assistants (coming often from a quite distant

24.text: country), and also among very poor families, who not infrequently are heedless

25.text: of the ties of relationship when they join their herds together to watch them

26.text: more effectually. Sometimes near relatives, even brothers, will sever their fire

27.text: from the family fire. When a house has been visited by misfortune and the

28.text: anger of “spirits,” — for instance, when many grown people or male children

29.text: belonging to it have died. — it may suddenly be cast out from the commu-

30.text: nity of fire. In this case the man who pronounces the protecting incantation¹

Footnote marker corrected from machine text's '!' (known ASCII substitution for a superscript digit, per catmus-substitutes-ascii-for-marks memory) to ¹, confirmed superscript on the raster.

31.text: may cut off the fire of the stricken family during the funeral ceremony, so

32.text: that others may not share in its bad fortune.²
32.note: Footnote marker corrected from machine text's '?' (ASCII substitution for superscript digit) to ², confirmed superscript on the raster.

33.text: The hearth is closely connected with the herd. The chief ceremonial of

34.text: the year, held early in the fall, represents the meeting of hearth and herd

35.text: after the summer’s separation. A large sacred fire is built, and the animals

36.text: are driven to it from the leeward side, so that the breath of the fire may

37.text: drive away the evil “spirits” that might come with the herd from the wilder-

38.text: ness. For the same purpose, burning fire-brands are thrown against the reindeer.
